# ARR Author Response Drafts — EMNLP 2026

Prepared 2026-05-20. Three predicted attack points with pre-drafted responses.

## Response #1: Single-Environment Generalization (Attack probability: 90%)

We thank the reviewer for this important observation. We distinguish between our **methodological contribution** (the diagnostic framework) and our **empirical finding** (death dominance in ScienceWorld). The quantitative results (DAF=90.4%, 78.9% label fraction) are specific to ScienceWorld, as stated in Limitations ¶1; the framework's generality claim is methodological.

Three lines of evidence support framework applicability beyond ScienceWorld: (1) **ALFWorld** (§3.4): the framework successfully diagnoses a qualitatively different mechanism—information asymmetry from admissible-action access (94.6% det-preferred, 0% death)—without any modification, demonstrating that the diagnostic procedure generalizes even when the dominant signal differs. (2) **MATH** (§3.4): the framework correctly identifies the absence of routing signal (p=0.81), a useful null result. (3) **MiniHack/Crafter** (§5): the framework correctly diagnoses two boundary conditions (no death mechanism; universal death without asymmetry). These are not failures—they are the framework performing its diagnostic function on environments where routing signal is absent or unexploitable.

Within ScienceWorld, extended validation on 5 excluded task types (n=100; Appendix S) yields DAF=0.991, confirming that task exclusion does not bias toward death-prone tasks.

## Response #2: Non-triviality / Novelty (Attack probability: 70%)

We thank the reviewer for this important observation. While the *direction* of death dominance may appear predictable given ScienceWorld's −100 penalty, three empirically verified predictions were not obvious a priori:

**(1) Intervention resistance across scales.** Qwen2.5-72B (10× parameters, independently collected at 72B for both strategies) reduces death rate to 30.6% but DAF *increases* to 92.4% (vs 7B's 90.4%). Scaling makes agents safer but does not reduce death dominance—a non-trivial outcome since one might expect larger models to diversify the signal beyond death avoidance.

**(2) Self-correction overcompensation.** Reflexion (N=3) yields DAF>100%: after self-correction, the internal strategy *outperforms* deterministic on non-death episodes (Δ_nd=−0.47), meaning death avoidance more than fully accounts for the entire performance gap. The routing signal is not merely death-dominated—it is *exclusively* death-driven after self-correction.

**(3) Inverted-U vulnerability.** A 0.5B model shows *reduced* death rate (13.3%) because it is too weak to reach dangerous states, suggesting capability and vulnerability are non-monotonically related.

These findings collectively show that death dominance is *resistant to reasonable interventions*—a conclusion that requires the precise quantification our framework provides.

## Response #3: Actionability / Practical Impact (Attack probability: 60%)

We thank the reviewer for this important observation. The practical contribution operates at the **meta-level**: before committing to router development in any new environment, practitioners can run our three-stage diagnostic pilot (Appendix R) using ~50 episodes (~2 GPU-hours) to answer: *Does routing signal exist? What drives it? Is a learned router worth building?*

This meta-question has concrete value. Our router training consumed ~200 GPU-hours without exceeding the always-deterministic baseline—an outcome the 50-episode pilot correctly predicted for all four tested conditions (always-deterministic, always-internal, random, trained router). The framework's diagnostic power lies not in building better routers, but in **determining whether router development is warranted** before investing in it.

The framework also provides deployment guidance: when DAF≈1 (as in ScienceWorld), always-deterministic is provably near-optimal (96.3% of oracle decisions match it), eliminating the need for runtime routing overhead entirely. When DAF≈0 (as in MATH), neither strategy dominates and routing has no value. The diagnostic thus converts an open-ended engineering question ("should we build a router?") into a quantitative decision with clear thresholds.

We acknowledge that our current validation covers one primary environment; applying the pilot procedure to additional environments remains important future work.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
In ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation, internal reasoning is error-prone---the model may hallucinate state changes (e.g., that water has boiled when the stove was never activated)---while deterministic external computation eliminates such errors via exact state transitions. The practical question: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision: Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} inserts API calls by perplexity reduction; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects heterogeneous modules per subtask; adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}; concurrent analyses further presuppose diverse routing signals~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026}. The shared assumption---that routing signal stems from diverse sources and a learned router can exploit it---has not been tested: no prior work has decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments.

We propose a \emph{diagnostic framework} comprising (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), which decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding. Under ScienceWorld's penalty ($P{=}100$), DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.1\%, 99.0\%]$). The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic death ($-100$ penalty); once death episodes are removed, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$ (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% tie rate; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). Our approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode outcomes.

Cross-context checks probe specificity: MATH Level~4--5 ($N{=}795$, code interpreter) shows no routing signal without catastrophic failure ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$); Llama-3.1-8B replication ($N{=}220$) confirms death dominance across model families (direction consistency 10/10; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}). Four intervention axes (retry, Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023}, $10{\times}$ scaling, action-space restriction) reduce death rates but none closes the gap to deterministic safety, with ${\geq}$12~pp residual gaps (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions: (1)~an \textbf{episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} that overcomes per-step oracle degeneracy (97.4\% tie rate), decomposes routing signal via penalty-independent (label fraction) and penalty-dependent (DAF) metrics, and predicts routing value from a ${\sim}$50-episode pilot (validated 4/4 conditions; Appendix~\ref{app:decision-framework}); (2)~applying this framework to ScienceWorld, we find that \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} stem from death asymmetry---a single mechanism that persists across four intervention axes and three model scales, contradicting the routing literature's implicit assumption of diverse signal sources (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}); (3)~\textbf{cross-model validation} (Llama-3.1-8B, DAF${=}88.2\%$), four intervention axes, and cross-environment boundary probes (MATH, ALFWorld) confirm the framework's diagnostic utility and the robustness of the finding (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).
